{"findings": [{"file": "src/ev/loop.zig", "line": 385, "severity": "major", "category": "correctness", "title": "The new `updateNow` comment claims owner-thread-only, but `setTimer` calls it from another thread", "body": "The added comment states: "Owner-thread only, so no timer lock: the cross-thread `clearTimer` never reads `now`/`tick`." `clearTimer` is not the only cross-thread entry point that reaches this state. `Loop.setTimer` (src/ev/loop.zig:622) calls `self.state.updateNow()` at line 636 and `armTimer` -> `nowFor` at line 647, both of which write `tick`, `now[0]` and `now_tick[0]`. The in-tree test "clearTimer racing a firing timer (cross-thread)" (src/ev/test/timer.zig:288) calls `loop.setTimer` from the main thread while the runner thread drives `l.poll(.max)`, and its own comment names `setTimer` as one of the "thread-safe" APIs. `setTimer` holds the timer mutex for those writes; the two `updateNow` calls in `poll` (lines 1392 and 1429) hold no lock. So two threads perform a plain, non-atomic read-modify-write of `tick` and plain writes of `now[0]`/`now_tick[0]` with no synchronization. This diff adds a second unlocked write site, which widens the window.

Mechanism of the worst interleaving: both threads read `tick` as T and both write T+1, so one scan increment is lost. The owner then writes `now[0] = t_new`, `now_tick[0] = T+1`; the `setTimer` thread afterwards writes `now[0] = t_old`, `now_tick[0] = T+1`. The final state is self-consistent (`now_tick[0] == tick`), so `nowFor(.awake)` does not refresh, and the whole scan runs against a timestamp older than the one the owner just read. The lost `tick` increment also leaves the lazy `boot`/`real` caches un-invalidated for that scan.

Consequence: `Loop.now()` and every `.duration` deadline armed in that scan are backdated, which is exactly the failure class this commit sets out to fix. It is also a data race that ThreadSanitizer reports. Either drop the cross-thread use of `setTimer` and say so in its doc comment, or take the timer lock (or make the fields atomic) in `updateNow`."}, {"file": "src/runtime.zig", "line": 776, "severity": "minor", "category": "performance", "title": "`tick_started_at` now predates the batch it timestamps, so the tick budget expires early", "body": "The new comment says the snapshot is refreshed "on return" from `loop.poll`. It is refreshed inside `poll`, at src/ev/loop.zig:1429, directly after `backend.poll` and before `processAsyncHandles`, `processCancelQueue`, `processCompletions` and the second `checkTimers`. All of those run completion callbacks, which push task wakes.

`tick_now` is stored into `self.tick_started_at` at line 791, and `spendQuantum` (line 679) compares a fresh `Timestamp.now(.monotonic)` against it. The stored value is therefore earlier than the true start of the task batch by the whole cost of the poll's completion processing. The previous code read the clock at line 778, after `poll` returned, which marked the real batch start.

Consequence: `elapsed` in `spendQuantum` is overstated by that offset, against a `tick_target_ns` of only 100 microseconds (line 643). Under a completion-heavy load the offset is a large fraction of the target, so `tick_expired` is set earlier than intended and the executor polls more often than the budget calls for. The EWMA retune at line 784 carries the same offset. If the cached snapshot is preferred for its lower cost, take the snapshot after the poll's callbacks run, or keep the direct clock read here."}, {"file": "src/ev/loop.zig", "line": 1392, "severity": "minor", "category": "tests", "title": "No test covers the new refresh at the top of `poll`", "body": "The diff adds `self.state.updateNow()` before `checkTimers`. Before it, `checkTimers` scanned against the snapshot taken at the end of the previous `poll`, so the snapshot was stale by the caller's whole task batch plus the previous poll's callbacks. A timer whose deadline passed during that batch was not seen as expired; instead `next_timeout` was computed too large by the staleness, the backend slept past the deadline, and the timer fired only on the post-poll `checkTimers` at line 1447, late by up to the batch duration.

That behaviour is observable and testable: run a long task batch (or a long completion callback), then call `poll` and measure when a timer whose deadline already passed fires. src/ev/test/timer.zig:303 shows the repository already pins the sibling defect (the post-poll refresh and `armTimer` backdating) with exactly this kind of regression test. The diff changes no test, so nothing fails if this line is removed again."}]}
